passage: Every reading hour at the village school, Parul slid the Hindi reader under her mat. The letters jumped about; ब and व looked like twins, and d and b swapped places in English too. "I'm stupid," she whispered to herself. But at home she fixed Dadaji's radio by watching how the wires ran, and she could repeat every story her cousin Simran told, word for word. One evening Simran read aloud while Parul followed with her finger. When Parul stumbled, Simran didn't sigh. "Your brain is quick, Parul. Only this part is hard. We'll go slow." The next week Simran went with Parul's mother to ask the teacher about extra reading help, before the school year ran on.

qa.q: What did Parul fix at home?
qa.a: Dadaji's radio, by watching how the wires ran.

qa.q: What does Parul's whisper 'I'm stupid' show about how she sees herself?
qa.a: It shows she has started to believe she is not clever because reading is hard, even though she is bright.

qa.q: Which choice by Simran protected Parul's confidence?
qa.a: Simran read slowly with her without sighing, told her that her brain is quick, and helped arrange early help at school.

qa.q: How might the teacher see Parul if Simran had not spoken up?
qa.a: The teacher might think Parul was lazy or careless for hiding the reader, and miss that she needs reading help.

grounding: It shows a bright child who stumbles over letters, hides her reader and thinks she is stupid, and patient early help that protects her confidence.

passage: On library day in the Cardiff school, Daniel always chose the thickest dinosaur book, then pushed it to the back of his cubby. The words swam. He mixed up "was" and "saw" and lost his place every line. But in the maker corner he built a working drawbridge from craft sticks and string before anyone else had finished their plan. Ms. Mina, the reading specialist, found the dinosaur book behind his lunch box. She didn't scold. She sat beside him with a coloured reading strip. "You figured out that drawbridge with no instructions," she said. "That's a strong brain. Reading is just a different puzzle for it. Want to try one page together?" Daniel laid the strip under the first line. Slowly, he read about a stegosaurus.

qa.q: What did Daniel build in the maker corner?
qa.a: A working drawbridge from craft sticks and string.

qa.q: Why might Daniel hide the dinosaur book in his cubby?
qa.a: He seems embarrassed and worried because the words swim and he loses his place, so he hides that reading is hard.

qa.q: What was the turning point when Ms. Mina found the hidden book?
qa.a: She didn't scold; she pointed to his strength, offered a reading strip and read one page with him.

qa.q: How might Ms. Mina see Daniel after the drawbridge and the hidden book?
qa.a: Ms. Mina likely sees a bright, capable builder who finds reading hard, not a lazy child, and believes one page together can help.

grounding: It shows a bright child who mixes up words and hides books, and a patient adult whose early help keeps his confidence.

passage: "Pooja beti, you think reading is easy for everyone? Let me tell you about a boy in Lucknow. Me. When I was nine, the letters jumped about like crickets. I hid my Urdu reader under the charpai and told my teacher the goat ate it. Everyone laughed, and I began to believe I was a duffer. But Master Hamid noticed that I could add sums in my head faster than anyone. He kept me back and said, 'A mind that fast is not stupid. We will read one page a day, slowly.' Every afternoon, one page. It took two years. Now look, I run the accounts for the whole market. So, your spelling test, na? We'll do it slowly." Wasim uncle folded his newspaper and opened her book.

qa.q: Where did Wasim hide his Urdu reader as a boy?
qa.a: He hid it under the charpai and told his teacher the goat ate it.

qa.q: How did young Wasim feel about himself before Master Hamid stepped in?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and began to believe he was a duffer, because the letters kept jumping and everyone laughed.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed things for young Wasim?
qa.a: Master Hamid noticed his quick mental sums, told him he was not stupid and read one page a day with him patiently.

qa.q: How might Master Hamid have seen young Wasim?
qa.a: Master Hamid saw a bright boy whose mind was fast and whose only difficulty was reading, not a lazy or stupid child.

grounding: An elder recalls being a bright child who stumbled over letters, hid books and thought he was stupid, until patient early help protected his confidence.

passage: Hafsa, nine, heard the substitute teacher say, "Everyone will read one paragraph aloud before the bell." Only ten minutes left. Her stomach dropped. The words on page forty were long and slippery; "was" kept looking like "saw." When her turn was three children away, she pushed her book into her bag and whispered, "I forgot it." At break she told her friend, "I'm stupid, that's why." Kunal Sir, the class teacher, had seen the book slide into the bag. He called Hafsa over at lunch. "You explained the water cycle better than anyone yesterday. Reading is hard work for you, not thinking." He phoned her Ammi that evening, and the next week Hafsa started reading sessions with the school's special teacher.

qa.q: What word kept looking like "saw" to Hafsa?
qa.a: The word "was" kept looking like "saw."

qa.q: How was Hafsa feeling as her turn to read came closer?
qa.a: She felt frightened and ashamed, so she hid her book and said she forgot it rather than read in front of everyone.

qa.q: What did Kunal Sir do that protected Hafsa's confidence?
qa.a: He told her she thinks well and only reading is hard, then called her Ammi the same evening so she could start extra reading help.

qa.q: If you were Hafsa's friend at break, how might you see her comment?
qa.a: You might feel sad and surprised to hear her call herself stupid, because she seems clever to you.

grounding: Shows a bright child who stumbles over words and letters, hides her book and thinks she is stupid, protected by early help and patience.

passage: In their Jaipur flat, Seema's brother Yash found three storybooks stuffed under her mattress. "Why are these here?" he laughed. Seema, eight, snatched them. "Because I hate them." At school that day she had written "bog" for "dog" and "dab" for "bad," and the class had giggled. Yet at dinner she explained exactly why the building's water tank overflowed and how to fix the float. Yash stopped laughing. "You're smarter than me at this stuff." Seema stared at her plate. "Then why can't I read?" The next day their mother met the school's reading teacher, who set up short daily sessions with coloured letter cards. Yash promised to stop teasing and sat with her during practice.

qa.q: Where did Yash find the storybooks?
qa.a: He found three storybooks stuffed under Seema's mattress.

qa.q: How did Seema feel when she asked, "Then why can't I read?"
qa.a: She felt confused and ashamed, unable to understand how she could be clever but still struggle with reading.

qa.q: What steps did the family take that could protect Seema's confidence?
qa.a: Their mother met the school's reading teacher for daily help, and Yash stopped teasing and sat with her during practice.

qa.q: How does Yash see Seema after dinner?
qa.a: Yash sees that Seema is smart, even smarter than him at practical things, and that her reading trouble is not about intelligence.

grounding: Shows a bright child who reverses letters, hides books and feels stupid, while family and school give early help and patience.

passage:
"Pema, why is your reading book under the cupboard?" Vasudha Miss asked after class.
"I lost it."
"It's right there."
Pema looked at the floor. "The words jump. B and d keep swapping. Everyone reads fast and I'm stuck on 'bridge'."
"That sounds really hard."
"I'm stupid, Miss."
"Pema, who told the whole story of the lost yak yesterday, with all the reasons why it ran away?"
"Me."
"Stupid children can't do that. Your brain is fine. Reading is just the tricky bit for you."
"So what do I do?"
"We start tomorrow: ten minutes with me each morning, bigger print, and a finger under each line. And I'll ask your parents about getting some extra help, early."
Pema pulled the book out from under the cupboard.

qa.q: Which word did Pema say was a sticking point?
qa.a: Pema said the word 'bridge'.

qa.q: Why did Pema hide the reading book?
qa.a: Pema felt ashamed and discouraged, because the words jump and Pema had started to believe being stupid was the reason.

qa.q: How did Vasudha Miss protect Pema's confidence?
qa.a: She reminded Pema of the strong storytelling about the yak, separated intelligence from reading, and started patient daily help plus early extra support.

qa.q: How might Pema's parents feel when Vasudha Miss talks to them?
qa.a: They might feel worried at first, then relieved that a teacher noticed early and has a plan.

grounding: Pema, a bright child who hides books and feels stupid, learns from the teacher that intelligence is intact and reading is the difficulty, with early, patient help.
